challenges.title: Whitespace Whisper
challenges.description:
A message that looks completely empty. It is not.

The file contains only invisible characters: zero-width spaces (U+200B) and zero-width non-joiners (U+200C), one bit per character.

**Goal:** decode the hidden text. A hex editor and patience are enough.

hints.text: Two distinct invisible characters means binary. Map one to 0, the other to 1.
Group the bits in eights, then read ASCII.

challenges.title: LSB Beginner
challenges.description:
A perfectly ordinary club poster. The least significant bit of every red channel spells something out — but only in the first row of pixels.

**Goal:** extract the bit string and read the flag. `zsteg` will get you there; doing it with Python and Pillow teaches you more.

hints.text: Read the red channel only, from the top-left, left to right.
Every 8 bits form one character. Stop at the closing brace.

challenges.title: Audio Ghost
challenges.description:
A 21-second recording of what sounds like a modem having a bad day. It is not a modem — it is Morse code, sent with two different tones.

**Goal:** decode the transmission. Listen, or analyse the waveform and measure pulse lengths.

hints.text: Short pulses are dots, three times longer are dashes.
Decode the tones: a dot is one unit long, a dash three. You get `SNT` followed by four tokens — submit `SNT{token_token_token_token}` in lowercase, with the digits kept as they are.

challenges.title: Polyglot File
challenges.description:
The image opens fine in every viewer. It is also a valid ZIP archive — the central directory lives after the image data, which is exactly why nobody noticed.

**Goal:** treat the file as an archive, extract the flag, and explain to a friend why MIME sniffing is not a security control.

hints.text: `binwalk` will show you two file signatures in one file.
Copy the file to `.zip` and try opening it — or carve from the `PK\x03\x04` offset.

challenges.title: Pixel Prison
challenges.description:
The payload is spread across the red channel, four bit planes deep, one bit per pixel in raster order. The rest is noise.

**Goal:** extract the bit stream and read the flag. The encoder that produced the image is attached — reading it is the intended path.

hints.text: `zsteg -a noise.png` will list candidate bit planes.
Read `encoder.py`. It tells you the channel, the bit position and the scan order in four lines.
